title: Waypoint
teaser: A retirement tracker with an agentic coach to simplify one question: "Am I on track for retirement?"

sections.problem: I wanted to explore how I could take an amortization calculator that many might use for retirement analysis, model more financial scenarios, implement far more Monte Carlo scenarios, and result in a justifiable number for whether a user is on or off track for retirement. Adding an agentic coach was there to serve as supplementary to a financial advisor and was aimed to especially think about what if scenarios that play out through the models, as in for every dollar put in a certain financial vehicle today, what it looks like at your desired retirement age along with how inflation impacts your purchasing power at that point.
sections.build: A retirement tracker built around a series of snapshots. It starts with who the person is and what they'd like to have at retirement, then each check-in logs their accounts and projects whether they're ahead, on track, or worth a closer look against the age and number they said they want. The projection comes from 1,000 simulated paths that replay 98 years of real US market history (1928 to 2025) rather than a single guess, and it's saved at each check-in so Waypoint can later compare what it predicted against what actually happened. Each projection records the assumptions it was built on, and the app flags one that has gone stale. A Detail view on the projection graph shows the work: the rates behind the number, a plain-language insight, and a year-by-year table with CSV export. An optional Coach writes a short assessment with one or two suggestions, aimed at pointing the user in a direction rather than handing down a verdict.
sections.technical: An HTML/JS front end running on a small Node.js/Express server, with settings and check-ins persisted to local JSON files and the projection engine kept in its own module. Each simulated year samples five-year stretches of a 60/40 stock-bond history, with inflation defaulting to that same period's 3.1% average so the today's-dollars result is consistent with the returns. Every projection and Coach analysis is stamped with its assumptions, and the Coach is told how the numbers were produced and only builds on earlier advice made on the same basis. The Coach is an agentic call to the Claude Code CLI on the user's own machine, and it sends the user's profile, balances, projection, notes, and recent analyses to Anthropic under their own account; everything else stays local. The public demo is a self-contained static build running the same projection math on a fictional persona, with one real Coach analysis generated on that persona's data and saved into the file.
sections.learning: The biggest challenge was simplification: letting a user bring difficult financial scenarios while the modeling stays behind the scenes. There is no right answer, per se, when running a whole host of Monte Carlo scenarios to arrive at a justifiable, defensible number, so keeping the build atomic enough to allow for sensible aggregation was the hardest part. Learning was also really working with the right balance of finding the agentic voice. Fine tuning the coach from not hallucinating too much but also not handing a user completely obvious information was the balance being sought. Where I eventually aimed the output was more akin to pointing a user in a certain direction and using the math to drive the "if then" portion of the justification of the recommendation. Version 2 taught me to justify the inputs, not just the output. The original 4 to 10% return band looked plausible but couldn't be defended, and testing it against 98 years of data showed its average was reasonable and its spread far too narrow. It also showed me that changing assumptions makes saved history misleading, so every result now carries the basis it was built on, and the model finally rests on a more defensible position.
sections.next: The next step is adding more robust financial vehicles to the mix, to further justify what the projections show and why. After that, I'd like to add more voices to the coach. I started with a balanced coach, but some users would likely prefer even softer treatment whereas other users would want more brass tacks from the coach to kick them into shape if they were off track. I also want to resolve an ambiguity hiding in plain words: the goal number is compared in future dollars, but a user may mean today's buying power.
